## Why

Repositories can ship shared `.codex/config.toml` settings, but developers need a private, higher-precedence file for local adjustments without editing checked-in config. The motivating case is disabling an inherited MCP server for one developer while preserving the repository default for everyone else.

This change was motivated by the local workarounds needed to override a checked-in `config.toml` at Figma. It also follows the spirit of `AGENTS.override.md` and Claude's `settings.local.json`.

## What changed

This PR adds project-local `.codex/config.override.toml` layers only.

- Load `config.override.toml` immediately after its sibling project `config.toml`.
- Reuse the project config-file loading pipeline for both sibling files, including trust handling, strict validation, project-key sanitization, relative-path resolution, warnings, and linked-worktree hook remapping.
- Merge override contents through the existing config-layer machinery, so partial nested tables such as `[mcp_servers.some_server] enabled = false` preserve lower-precedence fields.
- Surface override layers and field origins through app-server `config/read` metadata with a `projectOverride` layer source.
- Keep directory sidecars such as `hooks.json`, skills, exec policies, and standalone agent-role discovery anchored to the ordinary project layer so the sibling override does not scan the same `.codex` directory twice.
- Persist remembered MCP tool approvals to `config.override.toml` when the server is defined there, rather than creating or editing the shared sibling `config.toml`.
- Treat project overrides as developer-controlled network-proxy config and include them in the proxy's existing mtime reload watch list.

## Scope

This PR does not add user-level or system-level override files. It also does not copy ignored override files into linked worktrees; Codex App can handle that when it creates Git workspaces. General-purpose config live reload remains out of scope.

## Verification

- Regenerated app-server JSON and TypeScript schema fixtures.
- Ran focused core regressions for sibling discovery, precedence, nested MCP merge behavior, linked-worktree hook remapping, MCP approval persistence, and network-proxy handling.
- Ran the app-server `config/read` origin regression.
- Ran the `codex-config`, `codex-hooks`, `codex-core-skills`, and `codex-app-server-protocol` suites.

## Why

Runtime bundles must be installed in the environment where they will run. For a remote execution environment, app-server cannot download or unpack the runtime on its own machine and then return paths that only make sense on the executor.

This adds one app-server `runtime/install` flow whose orchestration stays in app-server/runtime-install logic while all target-local work is performed through the selected environment's existing generic `process/spawn` and filesystem primitives. Exec-server does not gain an install-specific RPC or a hidden installer command mode.

- Add the v2 `runtime/install` and `runtime/install/cancel` requests plus `runtime/install/progress` notifications. Installs are process-wide and serialized because there is one effective primary runtime installation at a time.
- Put install orchestration in `codex-runtime-install`, invoked from app-server with the selected `Environment`.
- Use generic executor processes for target-local platform discovery, archive download, checksum verification, archive listing/extraction, and atomic directory moves; use the executor filesystem API for validation, staging cleanup, metadata access, and resource publication.

## What

We'd like to start passing in stable item IDs for items that round-trip between Codex and Responses API.

There are two types of items:
- items that originate from the client (e.g. developer and user messages, among other things)
- items that originate from the server (e.g. assistant and reasoning messages, tool calls, etc.)

We now persist IDs in the rollout file for both. For client-originated items, we first generate IDs on the client. Historical items stored in rollout files without IDs will continue to be sent without an ID.

## Why

Codex replays Responses API input history across follow-up requests, websocket reconnects, compaction, resume, and fork flows. Since Codex uses `store: false` with OpenAI's Responses API, without persisting the item ID we will have no idea which items have round-tripped. Without stable IDs, the server is unable to recognize the same logical items since the IDs change. 

This is not really a problem for the server itself, but it complicates things downstream (in the data pipeline).

## ResponsesAPI item summary

**Client-generated items**:
- messages Codex itself creates, like user/developer/contextual messages
- function_call_output
- MCP tool outputs, which are sent as function-call outputs
- custom_tool_call_output
- tool_search_output when `execution == "client"`
- locally created assistant-role messages that still originate in Codex, like `InterAgentCommunication` and the review-mode exit assistant message

Those get Codex-generated prefixes like `msg_`, `fco_`, `ctco_`, and `tso_`.

**Server-generated items**:
- assistant messages returned by the model
- reasoning items
- compaction items
- function calls
- custom tool calls
- tool search calls
- local shell calls
- web search calls
- image generation calls
- tool_search_output when `execution == "server"`

## Compaction
An item ID stays the same across compaction only when the same `ResponseItem` survives into the replacement history. If Codex rebuilds equivalent text as a new item, it gets a new ID.

Concretely:
- **Local compaction:** effectively **no old response item IDs survive**. Codex extracts user-message text, builds new replacement `Message` items plus a new summary item, then assigns fresh Codex IDs. Same text, new items, new IDs.
- **compaction v1 with `/responses/compact`:** IDs survive for **server-returned items that Codex keeps**. In practice that means retained user/hook-prompt messages, any returned assistant messages, and returned compaction items keep whatever IDs the compact endpoint returned. Codex does not remint those. The **new** server-generated compaction item has an ID that is preserved after the boundary, but it did not exist before the boundary.
- **Remote compaction v2:** IDs survive for **retained prompt items copied into replacement history**. Today that is basically retained real user messages / hook prompts from the prior prompt. Those are cloned with their existing IDs. The server-generated compaction item keeps the ID from the `compaction_trigger` response. Mid-turn canonical context messages are newly rebuilt by Codex, so they get fresh IDs.

## What changed

- Added optional IDs to client-generated response input/output shapes and centralized Responses API ID generation in `codex-protocol`.
- Assign IDs when Codex creates new client-owned items, including user/developer/contextual messages and client-generated tool outputs.
- Preserve server-provided IDs for server-owned items and avoid synthesizing IDs for server-returned reasoning, compaction, assistant, tool-call, and other server-generated items.
- Attach available IDs into serialized HTTP, websocket, and compact request payloads for Responses API calls, including fields that are intentionally skipped by the normal serde shape.
- Persist available response item IDs into rollout JSONL so future resume/fork/replay keeps the same item identity, while legacy rollout items without IDs remain id-less when replayed.

## Verification

- Added protocol coverage for client ID generation, ID attachment, and preserving missing server IDs.
- Added targeted session coverage for preserving missing historical rollout IDs during resume.
- Added request, websocket, and rollout coverage for replaying persisted response item IDs.
- Added targeted compaction coverage for assigning IDs to new local compacted messages and mid-turn reinjected context.

## Manual testing

Given this modifies the way Codex calls ResponsesAPI, I had Codex exercise a locally built codex binary and exercise real threads, making sure that Responses API calls with item IDs still work as expected end-to-end.

Codex's summary:

> Manually validated the ChatGPT-auth path through `codex-backend` to prod Responses API by routing a local CLI build through a temporary forwarding proxy and inspecting the serialized request bodies sent to `/backend-api/codex/responses`.
> 
> Covered:
> - Initial Codex-authored prompt messages carried client `msg_*` IDs, and ordinary replay preserved prior prompt IDs plus server assistant IDs while assigning a new ID only to the new user message.
> - Client-generated `function_call_output`, `custom_tool_call_output`, and client-executed `tool_search_output` carried fresh `fco_*`, `ctco_*`, and `tso_*` IDs while replaying the corresponding server call IDs; prod accepted each flow.
> - Legacy `/responses/compact` and remote compaction v2, both manual and mid-turn, preserved retained/server-generated IDs across compaction and assigned fresh IDs only to Codex-rebuilt canonical context and new user messages.
> - Resume after remote compaction v2 replayed persisted compaction and retained-item IDs unchanged.
> 
> I did not manually validate `AgentMessage` end to end because the MultiAgentV2 prod path rejected encrypted tool configuration before any `agent_message` request was emitted.

## Why

Codex had `Stop` hooks, but no hook that fires specifically when an active turn is interrupted. Reusing `Stop` semantics would be misleading because interrupts are not stoppable: a handler can report advisory context, but it cannot block, continue, or otherwise change the interrupt path.

## What changed

Adds a root-turn `Interrupt` hook for turns that abort with `TurnAbortReason::Interrupted`, including active turns interrupted during shutdown. The hook runs after interrupt cleanup/rollout flushing and before `TurnAborted`, and v1 intentionally does not add a subagent-specific interrupt event, matcher support, or a public reason payload.

`Interrupt` uses a dedicated output contract instead of the shared `Stop` shape. Empty stdout succeeds, JSON with optional `systemMessage` is accepted, and control-style output such as `continue`, `decision`, `stopReason`, non-JSON stdout, invalid JSON, or exit-code `2` marks the hook run as failed without affecting the interrupt itself.

The TUI/app-server interrupt path now keeps the UI responsive while the hook runs and avoids duplicate hook execution from repeated interrupt inputs for the same active turn.

## Live preview

[Open PR #26259 in the internal CrabBox preview](https://eternal-main-oai-eternal-crabbox.devbox-2.gateway.internal.api.openai.org/pr/26259).

## Why

iTerm2's OSC 21337 status channel can show whether Codex is working, idle, or waiting for user input without replacing the terminal title. This is the base layer of the stack proposed by iTerm2 author George Nachman in #25879.

A Codex-owned background terminal can outlive the foreground turn. Treating that state as Idle makes OSC 21337 unsafe as an orchestration signal, so live background work must keep the tab Working.

## What Changed

- add a default-on `tui.tab_status` configuration switch
- emit OSC 21337 Working, Waiting, and Idle states from the TUI
- keep the tab Working while either a foreground turn or a tracked unified-exec process is active
- refresh status immediately when background processes start or exit, while preserving Waiting precedence
- clear only status fields Codex previously emitted when the TUI exits
- keep emission state isolated in a small bottom-pane state module
- add snapshot coverage for the foreground, background, Waiting, and Idle lifecycle

A panic or `SIGKILL` can leave the last tab status visible until another process overwrites it, matching the existing terminal-title limitation.

## How to Test

1. Run Codex in iTerm2 and start a turn.
2. Confirm the tab status changes from Working to Waiting for an approval prompt.
3. Start a background terminal command and let the foreground turn complete; confirm the tab remains Working.
4. Stop the final background process and confirm the tab becomes Idle.
5. Set `tui.tab_status = false` and confirm Codex emits no tab-status updates.

Targeted tests:

- `just test -p codex-config`
- `just test -p codex-tui tab_status`

## Stack

1. #26474 base OSC 21337 tab status (this PR)
2. [#26475](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/26475) flattened shell command display
3. [#26476](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/26476) detailed and throttled tab activity

## What?

- Carry nullable `parent_turn_id` from internal runtime handoffs through turn context and into emitted `codex_turn_event` analytics.
- Stamp only direct parent-to-child turn starts known by the runtime: v1/v2 multi-agent spawn and follow-up, CSV agent-job workers, delegated review, and Guardian review.
- Keep v2 mailbox transit metadata runtime-only with serde, schema, and TypeScript skips.
- Preserve the app-server connection for autonomous child turns so their analytics events emit.
- Add protocol, reducer, core, and app-server coverage for populated and null lineage.

## Why?

`parent_thread_id` identifies a child thread's lineage, but it does not identify the exact parent turn that triggered a child turn. Downstream analytics need that direct turn-level join when the runtime can prove it. Root turns and ambiguous handoffs keep `parent_turn_id = null`.

This does not block turn execution. The turn path attaches the id and enqueues analytics with `try_send`; reduction and HTTP delivery run in the existing background analytics worker. If the queue is full, Codex drops the analytics fact with a warning instead of waiting. The new awaited operations are bounded in-memory lookups for known child relationships and v2 mailbox lineage, not analytics delivery.

## How?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Parent turn has turn.sub_id"] --> B{"How does child work start?"}
  B -->|"v1/v2 spawn, follow-up, delegate, Guardian, agent job"| C["Submission.parent_turn_id = parent turn id"]
  B -->|"v2 turn-triggering mailbox message"| D["InterAgentCommunication.parent_turn_id runtime-only"]
  D --> E["InputQueue retains next trigger parent_turn_id"]
  E --> C
  B -->|"root or ambiguous work"| N["parent_turn_id = null"]

  C --> F["Build TurnContext.parent_turn_id"]
  N --> F
  F --> G["Build TurnResolvedConfigFact"]
  G --> H["try_send to analytics queue"]
  H --> I["Background reducer builds CodexTurnEventParams"]
  H -. "queue full" .-> X["Warn and drop analytics; turn continues"]
  I --> J["POST codex_turn_event with parent_turn_id"]
  J --> K["Companion PR materializes analytics.codex.fact_turns"]

  L["Child thread records inherited app-server connection"] --> I
```

The direct-parent value is turn-scoped rather than thread metadata because later child follow-up turns can be triggered by different parent turns. Queue-only v2 mail does not receive lineage unless it actually starts a turn.

## End-to-End Test

The manual scenarios below were captured on the same feature commits before the latest base-only rebase. Post-rebase focused validation is listed separately.

- Built the branch locally; the resulting CLI reported `codex-cli 0.0.0`.
- A one-shot `codex exec` spawned exactly one isolated child. Root turn `019ecde4-8722-77d3-987c-e5ce471307a2` produced child turn `019ecde4-aa09-7f20-a30c-bf21ecc9823b` with matching direct lineage.
- A fresh persisted session was resumed and then spawned a child. Resumed root turn `019ecde5-478e-7970-8f75-b42fe7dd0d0a` produced child turn `019ecde5-7332-7832-815a-a44761cc1fc7` with matching direct lineage.
- The rebuilt runtime was run against codex-backend from the companion PR. All 6 emitted analytics requests returned HTTP 200 with every event accepted and none skipped.
- In that combined run, root turn `019ecdf2-6106-7913-9870-87fcde7e6525` had null parent fields. Child turn `019ecdf2-7bd5-7be1-939f-525e5c077c51` had `parent_thread_id = session_id = 019ecdf2-5e30-7a40-ba35-fb21183a60ba` and `parent_turn_id = 019ecdf2-6106-7913-9870-87fcde7e6525`.
- The backend emitted both `Codex turn event params` logs after schema construction and analytics tracking.

## Post-Rebase Validation

Rebased onto `origin/main` at `b668abb488`.

- `codex-core parent_turn`: 5 passed.
- Analytics lifecycle, protocol serialization, delegate forwarding, and v2 follow-up focused tests: 4 passed.

## Motivation

Guardian review threads can cross the auto-compaction threshold between approvals. Without idle maintenance, the next approval request pays the full pre-turn compaction cost, adding many tens of seconds to its critical path. Running that work after a completed review gives compaction an idle-time head start while preserving the existing serial-review semantics and ensuring an uncertain Guardian trunk is never reused.

Tracks CA-540.

## Summary

- detect when a completed reusable Guardian session needs auto-compaction and start maintenance during the idle period
- quarantine the Guardian trunk before compacting it directly, and mark it reusable only after a new replacement-history compaction marker is durably observable
- treat in-flight eager compaction as a normal pre-review barrier bounded by the existing Guardian deadline; failed or non-durable compaction discards the trunk and falls back to a fresh ephemeral review
- serialize trunk claiming and removal through the maintenance latch and review permit so stale cleanup cannot remove a newly claimed trunk
- suppress Guardian-only out-of-turn maintenance markers when app-server reconstructs user-visible turns

## Testing

## Why

The existing `fs/readFile` and `fs/writeFile` methods materialize an entire file in one request. That is unsuitable for large files and remote app-server clients. Pull-based chunks provide bounded memory use, natural backpressure, cancellation between requests, and optional client-side pipelining without adding a separate push protocol.

Streaming writes should retain the behavior of the existing `fs/writeFile` API. Replacing the destination with a temporary file would change file identity, break hardlinks, discard executable bits and extended metadata, and potentially weaken custom Windows ACLs. The streamed API therefore opens the destination with ordinary create-or-truncate semantics.

A local benchmark measured strict pull at roughly 270 MiB/s and two-request pipelined pull at roughly 367 MiB/s, matching the temporary push implementation. The push API was therefore omitted.

## What changed

Add connection-scoped, client-supplied file handles to app-server v2 and exec-server:

- `fs/readFile/open`, `read`, `stat`, and `close` provide bounded positional reads.
- `fs/writeFile/open`, `write`, and `close` provide bounded sequential writes.
- Both local and remote exec-server filesystems implement the same handle interface.
- Read and write handles reject operations intended for the other handle type.
- Operations for one handle are serialized. Close waits for active work, rejects queued work, and prevents a pending open from becoming live.
- Remote handles close explicitly and report cleanup errors instead of relying on best-effort `Drop` requests.
- Each connection is limited to 64 opening or open file handles.
- Blocking local opens run on the blocking thread pool, and remote reads preserve the authoritative `eof` result.
- App-server schemas, TypeScript bindings, API documentation, and the API design document cover the new surface.

Opening a write handle creates or truncates the destination immediately. Completed chunks are visible immediately. Cancellation, disconnection, or an I/O error can leave a partially written file, matching ordinary truncate-and-write behavior. Existing destination identity and metadata are preserved.

## Summary

Adds workload identity federation to Codex CLI through the existing ChatGPT `ExternalAuth` path. After exchange, ordinary exec, TUI, app-server, Responses, tools, approvals, resume, and MCP flows consume normal in-memory ChatGPT auth; request code does not need WIF-specific branches.

- `codex-workload-identity` owns config, generic environment/file sources, RFC 8693 exchange, bounded responses, caching, refresh, principal pinning, and redaction.
- Provider SDKs remain isolated in dedicated provider crates. The standard CLI and app-server register the M1 Azure, AWS, GitHub Actions, and SPIFFE providers deterministically; repository policy forbids Cargo workspace feature maps because Bazel cannot model them reliably. Azure remains the first dogfood path.
- AWS accepts web identity and ECS/EKS container credentials only. It excludes static keys, profiles, SSO, credential processes, cached interactive identities, and EC2 IMDS.
- Project-local config cannot set `workload_identity`.

## Security boundary

External assertions and OpenAI access tokens remain in memory and are never written to `auth.json`. Configured credential environment variables are removed from model shells, shell snapshots, MCP registrations, and trusted hook/notify subprocesses. Credential files and SPIFFE sockets receive additive model-sandbox deny rules that survive approval escalation and danger-full-access mode; rotating projected-token symlinks deny their containing secret directory and any external canonical target.

WIF also prevents model subprocesses from recovering parent environment or memory. It enables Codex's process-inspection guard on Linux/Android (`PR_SET_DUMPABLE=0`) and macOS (`PT_DENY_ATTACH`); on Windows, WIF automatically selects Codex's existing restricted-token child sandbox instead of mutating the parent process DACL. WIF fails closed on other platforms where neither boundary is available.

Hooks remain explicitly trusted user/admin code. Environment scrubbing prevents accidental propagation, but this PR does not claim to isolate same-user hook code from Codex-owned files or process memory.

WIF fails closed over cached API keys and provider bearer tokens, and cannot bypass managed `forced_login_method = "api"`. A rejected token is discarded before forced refresh; proactive refresh may use the still-valid cached token only until its actual expiry.

Native metadata providers are intentionally excluded when Codex cannot prevent model subprocesses from reaching the same metadata endpoint. GCP projected tokens remain usable through the generic environment/file sources; native GCP metadata support is deferred pending endpoint isolation.

## Sources

| Type | Acquisition |
|---|---|
| `azure` | Reread `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` or an explicit absolute path |
| `aws` | Sign fixed STS `GetCallerIdentity` using web-identity or container credentials |
| `github_actions` | Request runner OIDC for the exact audience |
| `spiffe` | Request a JWT-SVID over a Unix Workload API socket |
| `environment` | Capture a named variable at Codex startup |
| `file` | Reread an absolute regular file, bounded to 1 MiB |

- The current binary used WIF to load managed cloud config and run the session while exchanging this devbox's Azure assertion exactly once (`req_150aa0eb4bf3b943a24f228c8f40a2a3`). - Azure exchange resolved the configured principal and completed real Responses tool turns under both workspace-write and danger-full-access.
- The model shell could access neither `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` nor the projected token file.
- WIF credential paths remained enforced by the sandbox but were absent from the full model-visible Responses request.
- A direct environment-token turn under unsandboxed danger-full-access could access neither the child variable nor the parent process environment through `/proc`.
- A projected Azure assertion supplied through a symlink could not be read through its external canonical target under danger-full-access; exchange and a real completion still succeeded.
- Required WIF is recognized as ChatGPT auth before the first exchange, preserving request attestation for WIF-only sessions.
- A custom provider with `requires_openai_auth = false` completed a Responses turn while WIF was deliberately configured with an invalid mapping; the fixture received no Authorization header.
- A custom unauthenticated provider and explicit `--oss` turn both succeeded with an unavailable WIF source; selecting the OpenAI provider with that same source still failed closed before model output.
- A config combining WIF with `forced_login_method = "api"` failed with the intended conflict before cloud bootstrap and produced zero AuthAPI token-exchange requests.
- A non-loopback HTTP token endpoint was rejected before cloud bootstrap; a local capture server received zero requests.
- After an app-server process warmed a two-second WIF token, removing the projected token and waiting for expiry did not break local `skills/list`; only optional workspace-plugin settings degraded to defaults.

## Summary

Clients need a durable thread-scoped API for adding and managing queued user messages. Dispatch ownership remains in `QueuedItemService`; app-server only converts wire values, calls the service, and maps extension invalidations to protocol notifications.

This change adds the experimental `thread/queue/*` API and its generated schemas behind `UserMessageQueue` / `user_message_queue`.

## API

- `thread/queue/add`
- `thread/queue/list`
- `thread/queue/delete`
- `thread/queue/reorder`
- `thread/queue/changed` invalidation notification

`TurnSubmissionParams` carries input, Responses API client metadata, additional context, and output schema. It carries no thread settings; queued messages use the thread's settings at dispatch time.

The initial API accepts `outputSchema` for submission-shape compatibility but intentionally discards it before persistence. Queued dispatch therefore has no final-output schema. Ordinary `turn/start` behavior is unchanged.

## Design decisions

- `TurnSubmissionParams` is the request type and `TurnSubmission` is the response type. Optional request fields may be omitted or sent as `null`, as with existing v2 thread `*Params` types; responses always include those fields and use `null` when no value exists. The separate types keep generated TypeScript and JSON Schema accurate even though their Rust fields are otherwise the same.
- Notifications contain only `threadId`. Clients fetch a bounded, paginated snapshot after invalidation.
- Capability discovery uses `experimentalFeature/list`, including effective per-thread configuration and runtime enablement.
- Queue RPCs validate the existing user-input limit and direct-input restrictions, then delegate to `QueuedItemService`.
- App-server constructs `QueuedItemService` once and shares that same `Arc` between the lifecycle extension and `ThreadQueueRequestProcessor`.
- Queued turns use the thread's current app-server client context at dispatch time. Producer identity lives in `QueuedItemProvenance`; the queue does not snapshot mutable session client state.
- The feature flag gates queue RPC admission. Work accepted before the flag is disabled may continue draining so durable rows are not orphaned.
- External provenance is `ExternalEvent { source, metadata }`; provenance describes origin and is not an authorization boundary.
- The generic typed app-server client already handles these request and notification variants, so no queue-specific client layer is required.
- Supporting queued output schemas is a follow-up that will pass turn-scoped configuration directly into turn-context construction rather than through `SessionSettingsUpdate`.

## Testing

Tests: payload handling, output-schema discard behavior, pagination, CRUD, runtime feature enablement, per-thread project config, archived and missing threads, direct-input restrictions, cross-client invalidations, and shared service wiring. Generated protocol artifacts are regenerated. Affected test targets compile locally; formatter and targeted clippy cleanup pass. Full suites run in CI.

## Stack

1. [#28264](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28264) - extract the core user-submission payload
2. [#28265](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28265) - accept user submissions at idle turn boundaries
3. [#28266](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28266) - add durable queue storage
4. [#28267](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28267) - dispatch queued messages through ordered idle extensions
5. **[#28268](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28268) - expose the app-server queue API (this PR)**
6. [#28307](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28307) - queue TUI follow-ups through app-server

## Summary

Adds managed `otel` support to `requirements.toml`, including composition across requirement sources and enforcement over ordinary config.

OTEL values use different composition rules depending on whether they are atomic or keyed.

## Why

Treating OTEL as either one scalar or one recursively merged object is unsafe. Scalars can be independent, exporters contain coupled endpoint/protocol/header/TLS settings, and metadata maps should compose without discarding unrelated entries.

This PR keeps layer composition, runtime enforcement, and telemetry validation in one reviewable contract.

## Semantics

- `log_user_prompt` and `environment` are independent exact values.
- `exporter`, `trace_exporter`, and `metrics_exporter` are each atomic:
  - the highest-priority specified exporter wins as a complete value;
  - endpoint, protocol, headers, and TLS are never mixed across layers;
  - a required exporter replaces the complete configured exporter.
- `span_attributes` composes by key; required values replace matching configured keys while unrelated keys remain.
- `tracestate` composes by member and field key.
- Required tracestate fields win; configured fields are retained only if the complete result remains W3C-valid.
- Invalid required trace metadata fails startup.
- Required exporter header names and values are validated during requirements application; errors identify the invalid header without exposing its value.
- Invalid configured metadata is rejected with a startup warning rather than erasing required metadata.
- A required exporter that cannot be constructed is fatal in app-server, exec, and TUI startup; optional configured exporters remain best-effort.
- Metrics export remains subject to the existing `analytics.enabled` gate.
- Valid conflicts produce a source-aware structured warning.

## Stack

## Summary

Extends the app-server config APIs to expose the managed settings implemented by the preceding PRs and prevents app-server config writes from mutating managed paths.

`configRequirements/read` returns authentication, storage, telemetry, shell environment, feedback, and Windows private-desktop requirements. `config/read` also reports the configured credential-store mode.

This PR contains the associated JSON and TypeScript schema regeneration.

## Why

Runtime enforcement does not require an API change, but clients need a safe view of the policies affecting effective configuration and a structured explanation when a write targets managed state. Keeping projection, write protection, and generated artifacts at the top of the stack isolates the mechanically large schema diff from the behavioral reviews below it.

## API semantics

`configRequirements/read` adds:

- `allowedLoginMethods`
- `allowedChatgptWorkspaces`
- `cliAuthCredentialsStore`
- `chatgptBaseUrl`
- `sqliteHome`
- `logDir`
- `modelCatalogJson`
- `checkForUpdateOnStartup`
- `otel`
- `allowLoginShell`
- `shellEnvironmentPolicy`
- `feedback`
- `windowsSandboxPrivateDesktop`

Additional behavior:

- OTEL exporter structure, header names, and TLS settings are preserved; header values are returned as `<redacted>`.
- Shell requirements use typed pattern-to-action filters and do not expose the removed profile-loading field.
- Nested feedback and Windows requirements are projected without changing runtime semantics.
- `config/read` returns credential-store mode as a typed value.
- Writes to a path managed by current or legacy requirements fail before persistence with `configRequirementReadonly`.
- Feature writes are rejected only when they target a specifically pinned feature; neighboring feature toggles remain writable.
- Key-path upserts retain the full path when merging so structured shell-environment reconciliation still runs.
- Existing requirement fields and normalization remain unchanged.

- Combined app-server JSON schema bundles

## Summary

Adds `shell_environment_policy` enforcement to `requirements.toml` using the keyed `filters` representation introduced at the bottom of this stack.

```toml
[shell_environment_policy]
inherit = "all"
ignore_default_excludes = false

[shell_environment_policy.filters]
"CORP_*" = "include"
"*SECRET*" = "exclude"
```

## Why

Managed shell policy must compose safely across requirement sources. Legacy arrays cannot compose per pattern because each higher layer replaces the entire array.

Ordinary `config.toml` continues accepting either representation to ease migration. `requirements.toml` accepts only keyed filters, isolating compatibility and making future array deprecation simpler.

## Semantics

- Requirements accept `filters` and reject legacy `exclude`/`include_only` arrays.
- `inherit` and `ignore_default_excludes` use the highest-priority specified value.
- `set` composes by environment-variable name; keys compose case-insensitively on Windows.
- `filters` composes by pattern; the highest-priority action wins for the same pattern.
- Required scalar leaves replace matching configured leaves.
- Required excludes and required default excludes remove configured `set` entries that would reintroduce a blocked variable.
- Required `set` entries are applied afterward and may deliberately re-add a variable.
- Required filters replace the configured action for the same pattern.
- Matching legacy-array entries are removed before installing a required action.
- Unrelated configured settings and patterns remain.
- Conflicts produce one source-aware warning for the structured shell policy.

This PR does not make shell snapshots policy-aware.

## `experimental_use_profile`

Review traced the runtime behavior to [#5278](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/5278), which silently removed the execution plumbing for shell-profile loading while leaving the config field behind. No usage regressions were reported after that removal, so this stack removes the inert `experimental_use_profile` / `use_profile` field rather than reviving it or exposing it through managed requirements.

[Codex Thread 019ed20e-8c96-7071-afcd-d8e4e82c45e7](https://codex-thread-link.openai.chatgpt-team.site/thread/019ed20e-8c96-7071-afcd-d8e4e82c45e7)

## Bug

Enterprise MCP administrators need the exact OAuth redirect URI before completing login so it can be pre-registered with the provider. Codex only constructed that final URI during login/browser launch, so the deterministic `callback_id`-suffixed redirect URI was not available as a standalone value. When `mcp add` used an ephemeral localhost callback port, the next login could also choose a different port unless that resolved callback base was saved.

## Fix

- Add `codex mcp callback-url <server-name>` to print the final redirect URI for an already-configured streamable HTTP MCP server when the URL can be known before OAuth starts.
- Print the final OAuth callback URL during `codex mcp add --url ...` for OAuth-supported servers from the same OAuth flow that launches the browser. This includes the actual OS-selected localhost port when the default callback port is ephemeral.
- Persist the resolved callback URL base after successful `mcp add` OAuth login under `[mcp_servers.<name>.oauth].callback_url`, so later login and `callback-url` calls reuse the same base and append the same deterministic callback ID suffix.
- Reuse the rmcp-client redirect URI construction path so the command, setup output, and login derive the same URL.
- Preserve the deterministic `callback_id` suffix for both configured callback URL values and local callback URLs.
- Return an actionable error from `callback-url` when the default callback URL cannot be precomputed because the callback port is ephemeral and no saved/configured callback URL exists.

## Safety / non-goals

- `callback-url` is read-only: it loads local config and prints the URL; it does not start OAuth, open a browser, mutate credentials, or perform network I/O.
- `mcp add` only persists the callback URL base after the existing OAuth flow succeeds; it does not change OAuth issuer validation, credential storage, callback routing, or provider interaction.
- Per-server `oauth.callback_url` overrides the global `mcp_oauth_callback_url` only for that server.
- Docs/config-comment wording is intentionally left out for the owning thread.

items.body:
## Why

A confirmed cross-host handoff incident showed `thread/fork` returning success after a transferred source rollout had a malformed JSONL record. The fork inherited only the parseable prefix of the source history, so completed turns after the malformed record silently disappeared while the destination thread looked usable.

The app-server fork path already receives source history through rollout/store hydration, but that hydration can tolerate and count malformed records. For `thread/fork`, a tolerated parse error is unsafe because it can create a partial destination.

## What changed

- `thread/fork` now validates the source rollout with `RolloutRecorder::load_rollout_items` before creating the fork.
- If the source rollout reports any malformed JSON/record parse errors, `thread/fork` returns an invalid-request error before calling `fork_thread_from_history`.
- Added a v2 regression test that corrupts a source rollout after an otherwise valid first turn and verifies the fork request fails without adding a partial fork to `thread/list`.

## Verification

- `just fmt`
- `just test -p codex-app-server thread_fork_rejects_malformed_rollout_without_partial_fork`
- `just test -p codex-app-server` was also run outside the filesystem sandbox. It completed with `861 passed, 17 failed, 1 skipped`; the remaining failures were outside `thread/fork` and included remote-control, descendant archive/delete, state-db/list, memory-mode, goal, and project-trust tests.

## Why

Plugin loading already parses plugin skills, but skill loading scans the same roots again during cold thread startup. Sharing raw per-root snapshots removes that duplicate filesystem and parsing work while preserving the existing skill-selection behavior.

## What changed

- introduce a shared `PluginSkillRootCache` keyed by the absolute plugin skill-root path
- populate the cache while `PluginsManager` resolves plugin capabilities, then reuse it from `SkillsService`
- bound the cache to 256 plugin skill roots and invalidate it alongside the existing plugin and skill caches
- keep non-plugin roots uncached and preserve root priority, deduplication, sorting, errors, and filesystem provenance when snapshots are merged

All plugin skills use `User` scope and the local filesystem, so the root path is sufficient cache identity.

This is stacked on #28608, which passes plugin namespaces directly into skill roots so the shared cache does not need to reprobe manifests.

## Why

`shell_command` still assumes that the Codex orchestrator owns the selected working directory and can spawn the command locally. In a split environment, the primary working directory and shell belong to the remote executor, so the command can run against the wrong filesystem or fail before reaching the executor.

Unified exec already routes commands through the selected environment. This change gives `shell_command` the same split execution boundary without changing its local execution path.

## What this achieves

- Resolves the command working directory and shell from the primary turn environment.
- Keeps the existing `shell_command` approval and sandbox transformation flow.
- Sends remote commands through the existing unified-exec process lifecycle and environment exec backend.
- Avoids applying orchestrator-local shell snapshots and runtime path changes to remote commands.
- Leaves local `shell_command` execution unchanged.
- Adds an integration test proving that a remote primary environment reads the remote working directory instead of the local one.

## Known limitations

Remote `shell_command` intentionally supports no more than unified exec currently supports on the split:

- Remote stdout and stderr are exposed as unified exec's combined output stream; stderr identity is not preserved separately.
- Timeout and cancellation begin after the remote process is established, and termination uses unified exec's existing output-drain behavior.
- Sandboxing and platform support are the same as unified exec today. This PR does not improve split sandboxing or Windows support.
- Remote shell snapshots and the zsh-fork execution path are not supported.
- Remote paths must currently be representable using the orchestrator's native path convention.

## Why

`built_tools` repeatedly reconstructs stable hosted-connector and curated-plugin source fragments even when their owners have not changed. The safe reuse boundary is an owner-issued generation over a complete immutable source snapshot—not a content hash, incidental object identity, or a UI cache invalidation.

This adds the smallest session-scoped consistency layer at the real runtime seam while keeping refresh, account context, network fetches, plugin materialization, directory discovery, policy, and final router construction with their existing owners.

- add `RuntimeToolCatalogManager` and immutable `RuntimeToolCatalogSnapshot` with two explicit top-level slots: `hosted_connectors` and `revisioned_plugins`
- give the host-owned `codex_apps` MCP runtime snapshot an opaque monotonic generation that advances on manager construction, successful hosted startup, and every successful hard tools refresh
- have `PluginsManager` publish complete local-curated and `openai-curated-remote` snapshots with opaque monotonic generations
- advance local curated after a successful repo sync plus curated cache refresh; advance remote curated after a successful global directory refresh
- key remote-curated ownership to the same base URL/account/user/workspace context as its disk cache, so account-context replacement cannot reuse another account's fragment

## Why

The filesystem fallback for `thread/list` reads a rollout summary before it can reject a thread by `SessionMeta` fields such as `source`, `model_provider`, or `cwd`. A directory with many subagent rollouts therefore makes an interactive-thread query parse thousands of summaries that it will discard.

## What changed

- Bound rollout discovery and modification-time reads to the existing 10,000-file scan limit for nested and flat layouts.
- Read filtered rollouts once: inspect `SessionMeta`, reject non-matches, and continue summary extraction from the same open reader for accepted rollouts.
- Build candidates in batches sized to the remaining page plus one lookahead instead of always building 64 summaries.
- Add operation-count tests and ignored release benchmarks for interactive, compressed, and power-user workloads.

The change does not alter the rollout format, SQLite schema, app-server protocol, pagination cursor, or result ordering.

## Benchmark

Each result is the p50 of 20 serial runs from a release build on the same machine. The 5,100-rollout case creates 5,000 rejected subagent rollouts followed by 100 interactive rollouts. It is intentionally a power-user stress case rather than a typical user profile.

## Summary

- add a periodic app-server worker that refreshes the Codex Apps MCP tools cache every five minutes
- extend the shared periodic worker with an explicit delayed-first-run policy
- reload effective config for every pass and reuse the existing threadless connector refresh path, feature/auth gates, MCP runtime config, and disk/in-memory caches
- stop the worker during normal app-server shutdown and background-task draining

## Scheduling and RPC interaction

The first background apps pass waits five minutes because app/list already populates the cache on demand. This avoids racing startup app/list or forceRefetch requests. Later background passes force a tools-cache refresh; normal app/list requests continue using the existing cache, while explicit forceRefetch retains its current bypass semantics.

This PR refreshes accessible Codex Apps tools. It does not force-refresh the separate connector directory cache.
